questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} & =\frac{\sqrt{0+4}-2}{0}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\sqrt{x+4}-2)(\sqrt{x+4}+2)}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x+4-4}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{0+4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to }\frac{8-\sqrt{8x}}{x-8} & =\frac{8-\sqrt{8(8)}}{8-8}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 8}\frac{8-\sqrt{8x}}{x-8} & ={lim}_{x\to 8}\frac{(8-\sqrt{8x})(8+\sqrt{8x})}{(x-8)(8+\sqrt{8x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 8}\frac{{8}^{2}-(\sqrt{8x})^{2}}{(x-8)(8+\sqrt{8x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 8}\frac{64-8x}{(x-8)(8+\sqrt{8x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 8}\frac{-8(x-8)}{(x-8)(8+\sqrt{8x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 8}\frac{-8\cancel{(x-8)}}{\cancel{(x-8)}(8+\sqrt{8x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 8}\frac{-8}{8+\sqrt{8x}} \\  & =-\frac{8}{8+\sqrt{8(8)}} \\  & =-\frac{8}{8+8} \\  & =-\frac{8}{16} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-2}{{x}^{2}-9} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-2}{(x-3)(x+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(\sqrt{x+1}-2)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)}{(x-3)(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{(\sqrt{x+1})}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x-3)(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x+1-4}{(x-3)(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{(x-3)(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{1}{(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(3+3)(\sqrt{3+1}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=0$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+5}-\sqrt{5}} & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{0+5}-\sqrt{5}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+5}-\sqrt{5}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+5}+\sqrt{5})}{(\sqrt{x+5}-\sqrt{5})(\sqrt{x+5}+\sqrt{5})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+5}+\sqrt{5})}{{(\sqrt{x+5})}^{2}-{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+5}+\sqrt{5})}{x+5-5} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+5}+\sqrt{5})}{x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\sqrt{x+5}+\sqrt{5}) \\  & =\sqrt{0+5}+\sqrt{5} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{z\to 6}\frac{z-6}{\sqrt{3z-2}-4} & =\frac{6-6}{\sqrt{3(6)-2}-4}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{z\to 6}\frac{z-6}{\sqrt{3z-2}-4} & ={lim}_{z\to 6}\frac{(z-6)(\sqrt{3z-2}+4)}{(\sqrt{3z-2}-4)(\sqrt{3z-2}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{z\to 6}\frac{(z-6)(\sqrt{3z-2}+4)}{(\sqrt{3z-2})^{2}-{4}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{z\to 6}\frac{(z-6)(\sqrt{3z-2}+4)}{(3z-2)-16} \\  & ={lim}_{z\to 6}\frac{(z-6)(\sqrt{3z-2}+4)}{3z-18} \\  & ={lim}_{z\to 6}\frac{(z-6)(\sqrt{3z-2}+4)}{3(z-6)} \\  & ={lim}_{z\to 6}\frac{\sqrt{3z-2}+4}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3(6)-2}+4}{3} \\  & =\frac{4+4}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=1$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x-1}{x-\sqrt{x}} & =\frac{1-1}{1-\sqrt{1}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x-1}{x-\sqrt{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{(x-\sqrt{x})(x+\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{{x}^{2}-{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{{x}^{2}-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{x(x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x+\sqrt{x}}{x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{1+\sqrt{1}}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=\frac{1}{4}$ we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{4x-1}{2x-\sqrt{x}} & =\frac{(4\cdot \frac{1}{4}-1)}{(2\cdot \frac{1}{4}-\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}})}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{4x-1}{2x-\sqrt{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{(4x-1)(2x+\sqrt{x})}{(2x-\sqrt{x})(2x+\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{(4x-1)(2x+\sqrt{x})}{(2x)^{2}-(\sqrt{x})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{(4x-1)(2x+\sqrt{x})}{4{x}^{2}-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{(4x-1)(2x+\sqrt{x})}{x(4x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{\cancel{(4x-1)}(2x+\sqrt{x})}{x\cancel{(4x-1)}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{2x+\sqrt{x}}{x} \\  & =\frac{(2\cdot \frac{1}{4}+\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}})}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{x-2\sqrt{x}}{x-4} & =\frac{4-2\sqrt{4}}{4-4}=\frac{0}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\eqalign{
	\lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x - 2\sqrt{x}} {x - 4} &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {(x -2 \sqrt{x})(x+2\sqrt x)} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
            &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x^2-\left(2\sqrt{x}\right)^2} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x^2-4x} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x(x-4)} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x} {x+2\sqrt x} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {4} {4+2\sqrt4} \
	    &=\dfrac 1 2.
	}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=0$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{3x}{\sqrt{x+1}-1} & =\frac{3\cdot 0}{\sqrt{0+1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac {3x} {\sqrt{x + 1} - 1} 
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{(3x)(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{x + 1} - 1)(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{\left(\sqrt{x+1}\right)^2-1^2}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{x+1-1}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{x}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}3(\sqrt{x+1}+1)\
&=3(\sqrt{0+1}+1)\
	&=6.
}
$$
